children: As surging diesel and gasoline prices demonstrate, global refining capacity is tight. So far, the U.S. has been a source of steady refining. But what if American refineries have been running too hard?

On Monday, ExxonMobil said that it had to shut down its Joliet refinery in Illinois after a power outage, according to OPIS. The outage occurred around 3:30 p.m. Central Time on Sunday, with power restored around 7 p.m. The refinery has a capacity of 275,000 barrels a day and makes up about 6% of overall refining capacity in the Midwest, according to the company's fact sheet.

In this case, it is unclear whether the outage was related to a lack of maintenance given that Exxon pointed to power issues. But it is a reminder that the world's already-tight refining market doesn't have much room for error. Refining capacity in two major fuel-exporting regions, the Middle East and Russia, has been curtailed by conflict. In August, global refineries processed 4.2 million barrels a day fewer than a year earlier, according to the latest report from the International Energy Agency.

With fuel margins at record highs, U.S. refineries have been running near full speed to capture profits. They have been running at higher than 97% utilization capacity over the past four weeks, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. By comparison, utilization has run at an average of 93% to 94% at this time in the last four years.

This month is typically the start of a fall maintenance season, but as of the first week of September, U.S. refineries were still running hard at about 98% utilization. With fuel markets already on edge, that high utilization rate could become yet another risk if U.S. refineries reach their breaking point.
